title: Unions, intersections, discriminated unions
subtitle: | vs &, literal tags, exhaustiveness with never

cards.front: Why are unions and discriminated unions a core TS pattern?
cards.meaning: They are the most important day-to-day modeling pattern for async UI state, API results, and domain events: alternatives in the domain become a union, then a literal tag, then safe narrowing.
A value of type A | B is either an A or a B (or both if a value happens to satisfy both — rare for primitives). Unions mean “one of these.”

cards.front: On string | number, why is x.toFixed() an error?
cards.meaning: toFixed is not on string. Until you narrow, you may only use operations valid for every constituent.

cards.front: Cat | Dog — why can't you call meow()?
cards.meaning: On a union of objects you may only access members that exist on every constituent until you narrow. Use in, a discriminant, or a type guard before variant-specific methods.

cards.front: Why model alternatives as a union instead of optionals?
cards.meaning: Unions model real alternatives without lying with optionals like data? plus error? on one blob. Invalid combinations stay unrepresentable if you use variants instead of one optional-field bag.
A value of type A & B must satisfy both A and B at once — “all of these at once.” It is not a substitute for or; that is a union.

cards.front: What is { name: string } & { age: number } effectively?
cards.meaning: An object type with both fields: { name: string; age: number }. Use intersections to compose object capabilities (Writable & Timestamped) or mix in cross-cutting fields.
cards.example: type NameAndAge = { name: string } & { age: number }

cards.meaning: That resolves to never because no runtime value is both string and number. Call out this trap in interviews.

cards.front: Intersecting objects with the same property but incompatible types?
cards.meaning: Tends toward never for that property. Same idea as string & number: the intersection asks for something no value can satisfy.
Compose object capabilities and mix in cross-cutting fields. Do not use & when you meant “or” — that is a union.

A type that admits only specific primitive values, such as 'loading' | 'success' | 'error', Dice = 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6, or Bit = 0 | 1. String/number/boolean literals are the usual tags for discriminated unions.
Without as const or an annotation, s might widen to string. t is a literal type. Widening to string weakens discriminant narrowing.
cards.example:
const s = 'success'; // might widen to string
const t: 'success' = 'success'; // literal type

cards.front: Why as const on objects for tagged values?
cards.meaning: as const on objects freezes literal inference for fields — useful when building tagged values so status stays 'success' instead of string.
A union of object types that share one property — the discriminant — with distinct literal types per variant. Checking that tag lets TypeScript narrow the whole object safely.
cards.example:
type FetchState = LoadingState | SuccessState | ErrorState
// status: 'loading' | 'success' | 'error'

cards.meaning: Loading has only status: 'loading'. Success has status: 'success' and data: User. Error has status: 'error' and error: string. The union is FetchState = those three.
When you check the discriminant, TypeScript eliminates other variants. Properties unique to the remaining variant become available — no cast. success sees data; error sees error.
cards.example:
case 'success': return state.data.name; // SuccessState
case 'error': return state.error; // ErrorState

cards.front: Why not { status: string; data?; error? }?
cards.meaning: Invalid combos like { status: 'success', error: 'oops' } are still typeable — the type does not encode valid combinations. With a discriminated union, each variant only carries fields that belong together; construction and reads are enforced, and exhaustiveness with never catches missed cases when the union grows.

Shared name for the tag (status, type, kind, tag). Literal (or other unit) types that do not overlap across variants. Prefer required tag fields — optional tags weaken narrowing. Keep each variant's exclusive data on the right branches only.
status: string is not a literal, so equality checks do not usefully narrow. Use string literal unions (or as const) so each variant's tag is a distinct literal TypeScript can eliminate.

cards.front: Same literal tag on two variants?
cards.meaning: Fails as a clean discriminant. Tags must not overlap across variants, and the tag must not be missing on some members.

cards.front: Tag missing on some union members?
cards.meaning: Not a clean discriminant. Every variant should carry the shared required tag with a distinct literal.

If FetchState later includes { status: 'cancelled' } and you forget a case, state in default is that leftover variant — not never — so assertNever(state) fails to compile. That is the reliable “fail compile on new variant” technique.
never is the bottom type: no value should exist there. Assigning something to never is only legal if the checker proves the code is unreachable / fully handled.

cards.front: Is a switch exhaustive without default/assertNever?
cards.meaning: Not reliably. A switch that returns in every known case may still not error when a new union member is added, depending on control-flow and return types. assertNever in default is the reliable compile-fail when a variant is added.

cards.front: Can you narrow a discriminant with if, not only switch?
cards.meaning: Yes. Same discriminant idea: if (state.status === 'success') { state.data } is OK. switch is not required.

cards.front: How do discriminants relate to typeof / in / predicates?
cards.meaning: Other narrowing appears in depth in the narrowing unit. Discriminants are the object-oriented form of the same idea: a runtime check eliminates variants in control flow.
A union of function types is callable with args common to all; the return type becomes a union. Awareness only — not a full overloads course.
Intersection of functions behaves differently (overloads-like). Do not casually intersect call signatures without reading the errors — prefer explicit overloads or discriminated args.

cards.front: Naming FetchState = Loading | Success | Error — keyword?
cards.meaning: Use a type alias. A top-level union of variants cannot be expressed as a single interface alias; interfaces are for object shapes. Related: unions need type from the type-vs-interface unit.
Classic mix-up of “or” vs “and.” Union is one of these; intersection is all of these at once.
Error (or unsafe if you cast). On a union you only get common members until you narrow with the tag, in, typeof, or a predicate.

cards.front: How do alternatives become exhaustiveness checks?
cards.meaning: Domain alternatives → union type → literal tag per variant → discriminated union → narrow on tag → assertNever for exhaustiveness. Intersection combines requirements and conflicts go to never. A type alias (not interface) names the union.

cards.front: What should you be able to do in an interview on this unit?
cards.meaning: Define | vs & with a one-line example each. Build a three-state async FetchState and narrow on status. Explain why tagged unions beat optional bags. Show assertNever and what breaks when a variant is added. Call out string & number → never.
